allNodeData.name: Energy Time Uncertainty Principle
allNodeData.description: Energy

allNodeData.name: Blocks
allNodeData.description:
- When blocks are in contact and they do not exert forces on eachother it is generally good to treat them as a single object

- When they exert forces on eachother you must treat them individually

Common question types:
- blocks on angled ramps
- blocks on angled ramps with pullys/springs
- blocks in contact falling
- blocks being pushed on a table with friction between them
- pulleys
- blocks connected and suspended on a string

For the purposes of the GRE a massless string carries the $same$ tension at every point on the string.

allNodeData.name: Energy
allNodeData.description:
- great if you want to know how fast or how far something goes, (i.e. boundary states not full time dependent descriptions)

Obvious energy terms you should know:
Translational: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$
Rotational: $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$
Gravitational Potential: $mgh$
Spring potential: $\frac{1}{2}kx^2$

Potential energy is defined up to an additive constant, you can pick any origin as long as you remain consistent with signs

For any conservative $F$, the change in potential energy $\Delta U$ between points $a$ and $b$:

$\Delta U=-\int_a^bF\cdot dl$

$F = -\nabla U$

Gravitational force: $\frac{GMm}{r^2}$

Some questions:
 - block on ramp of strange shape and frictionless surface

Note for potential energy:
- signs on $U$ can be a bitch, best advice is to consider the value of the potential as you very the independent variable. For example: if your potential is a gravitational field, you know that the actual signed value of potential should be increasing ($\textbf{Not}$ the magnitude). So the sign of potential may change with what you are measuring it from, but the actual signed value of potential should increase in a gravitational field with height.

allNodeData.name: Approximations
allNodeData.description: - $g$ should always be approximated to 10 unless specified otherwise

allNodeData.name: Kinematics
allNodeData.description:
Primary problem types:
- projectile motion
- reference frame problems
- uniform circular motion
- nonuniform circular motion
  - roller coaster
  - vertical pendulum attached to a rigid rod making a revolution
- rolling without slipping ($v=\omega R$)
Tips:
- sometimes it is helpful to use work/energy expressions instead of just kinematic ones.
- it is almost always faster to solve motion problems with energy instead of kinematics. its only necessary when you need to know the explicit time dependence of a system, y(t), x(t) etc.
- generally speaking, if time doesn't appear in the problem, you can leave kinematics out.

allNodeData.name: Moment of Inertia
allNodeData.description:
$I = \int r^2 dm$

Particle: $MR^2$

Sphere (About center axis): $\frac{2}{5}MR^2$

Cylinder: $\frac{1}{2}MR^2$

allNodeData.name: Parallel Axis Theorem
allNodeData.description:
The moment of inertia about an axis parallel to one going through the center of a body is equal to:

$Mh^2+I_{cm}$ 

where $I_{cm}$ is the moment of inertia through the body's center of mass and $h$ is the distance between the 2 axes.

allNodeData.name: Work Energy Theorem
allNodeData.description:
$E_{initial}+W_{other}=E_{final}$

$W=\Delta{KE}$

$W=\int F \cdot dl$

allNodeData.name: Momentum
allNodeData.description:
Momentum is always conserved in a system without external forces. When an external force is present we have:

$F=\dot{P}=\frac{dP}{dt}$

$\tau = r\times F = \dot{L}=\frac{dL}{dt}$

$L = r \times p$

$L = I\omega$ (extended body)

Non-Inertial Frames:

 $F_{centrifugal} = -m\Omega^2r$

 $F_{Coriolis} = -2m\mathbf{\Omega}\times v$

Typical problems:
 - Collisions:
  - Perfectly Elastic: Energy is conserved 
   - do NOT assume a collision is perfectly elastic unless stated explicitly
  - attempt "limiting cases" and "dimensional analysis" before doing algebra.
 - merry go rounds
 - spinning disks
 - puck spinning from hole in middle of table

allNodeData.name: Center of Mass
allNodeData.description:
$r_{CM}=\frac{\int \mathbb{R} dm}{M}$

or discrete:

$r_{CM} = \frac{\sum\limits_{i=1}^N r_i m_i}{M}$

allNodeData.name: Largrangian Mechanics
allNodeData.description:
Problems fall into 2 categories:
 - Write down the Lagrangian or Hamiltonian function
 - Write down the Lagrangian or Hamiltonian equations of motion

Recipe for computing $T$:
 - Write down expressions for Cartesian coordinates in terms of your chosen coordinates $q$
 - Differentiate the Cartesian coordinates ($x,y,z$) with respect to time to get $(\dot{x},\dot{y},\dot{z})$, paying careful attention to the chain rule.
 - Form the expression for the Cartesian kinetic energy:

$T=\frac{1}{2}m(\dot{x}^2+\dot{y}^2+\dot{z}^2)$

for a point particle or:

$T=\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

for an extended object.

allNodeData.name: Lagrangian
allNodeData.description:
$L(q,\dot{q},t)=T-U$

Where $T$ is total kinetic energy of the system, $U$ is the potential energy, and $q$ is the collection of all the coordinates describing the degrees of freedom of the system.

allNodeData.name: Euler Lagrange Equation
allNodeData.description:
$\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}$

The momentum conjugate to $q$ is the quantity:

$p_i = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}}$

Note that if $\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}=0$, that is $L$ is $independent$ of $q$, $\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}}$, the momentum conjugate, is conserved.

allNodeData.name: Hamiltonian Mechanics
allNodeData.description:
$H(p,q) = \sum\limits_i p_i\dot{q}_i-L$

or

if $U$, the potential, does not depend explicitly on velocities or time:

$H = T + U$

Hamiltonian equations:

$\dot{p} = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial q}$

$\dot{q} = \frac{\partial H}{\partial p}$

If and only if the hamiltonian is independent of a coordinate $q$, the corresponding conjugate momentum $p$ is conserved.

allNodeData.name: Effective Potential
allNodeData.description:
Deriving the Lagrangian in spherical coordinates yields:

$L=\frac{1}{2}m[\dot{r}^2+r^2\dot{\phi}^2+r^2\sin^2\phi\dot{\theta}^2]-U(r)$

Restricted Lagrangian for particle orbiting in a plane:

$L=\frac{1}{2}m\dot{r}^2+\frac{1}{2}mr^2\dot{\phi}^2-U(r)$

We can now solve the E.L.E for $r$ and perform some manipulation to get:

$V(r)=\frac{l^2}{2mr^2}+U(r)$

Where $V(r)$ is "effective potential".

When 2 bodies orbit eachother, we replace $m$ with the reduced mass:

$\mu=\frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}$

When one mass is much larger than the other this reduces (approximately) to the smaller mass.

With our effective potential we get the energy:

$E=T+V=\frac{1}{2}m\dot{r}^2+\frac{l^2}{2mr^2}+U(r)$

Orbit shapes:

$E \gt 0$ - Hyperbolic Orbit
$E = 0$ - Parabolic Orbit
$E \lt 0$ - Elliptical Orbit
$E = V_{min}$ - Circular Orbit

Notes:
The effective potential reformulates orbital motion so that:
 - The angular momentum terms in the kinetic energy appear instead as a centrifugal barrier in the potential energy.
 - The motion in $r$ behaves like a 1-D particle in $V_{eff}(r)$
 - Stable orbits correspond to minima of $V_{eff}(r)$
In short, the effective potential converts the kinetic energy of rotation into an equivalent “centrifugal” potential energy term, making orbital dynamics much easier to analyze.

allNodeData.name: Springs and Harmonic Oscillators
allNodeData.description:
Hooke's Law:

$F=m\ddot{x}=-kx$

$U(x) = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$

Equations of motion for simple oscillators of this type take the form:

$x(t)=Acos(\omega t + \phi)$

or

$x(t) = Ae^{i\omega t}$

with $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$

Springs:
 - Try limiting cases, dimensional arguments, and symmetry
 - Try conservation of energy
 - Try writing down a differential equation and solving it

Effective Spring Constant:

Same as capacitors:

Parallel $k_{eff}=k_1+k_1+...+k_n$

Series: $k_{eff}= \frac{1}{\frac{1}{k_1}+\frac{1}{k_2}+...+\frac{1}{k_n}}$

allNodeData.name: Kepler's Laws
allNodeData.description:
- Planets move in elliptical orbits with one focus at the Sun
- Planetary orbits sweep out equal areas in equal times.
- If $T$ is the period of planetary orbit,  and $a$ is the semi-major axis of the orbit, then $T=ka^\frac{3}{2}$, with $k$ the same constant for all planets.


its a natural consequence of angular momentum for radial potentials (I.e. conservation of angular momentum):
$l=mr^2\frac{d\phi}{dt}$

$\frac{l}{m}dt=r^2d\phi$

$T=ka^\frac{3}{2}$

with:

$k=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{G(m_{planet}+m_{sun})}}$

allNodeData.name: Normal Modes
allNodeData.description:
Most likely:
 - n masses attached to springs

Shortcut approach:

$q_k(t)=a_ke^{i\omega t}$

$0=det(A_{jk}-\omega^2m_{jk}a_k)$

Basically just assume $\ddot{x}=-\omega^2x$ and plug it into E.O.M

solving the eigenvalue problem for some real values $A$ gives:

$X(t)=Acos(\omega t)$

Notes:
When assessing coupled linear systems we often take (for small displacements) that: The force on particle $j$ due to a displacement of particle $k$ is equal to the force on particle $k$ due to the displacement of particle $j$.

$M^{-1}\frac{d^2X}{dt^2}=-KX$

$Z(t)=Ae^{-i\omega t}$ is a solution if:

$\omega^2 A = -M^{-1}KA$

Process:
- Write down the equations of motion for the system
- Determine the matrices $A_{jk}$ and $m_{jk}$ and write down the secular equation
- solve to find the normal frequencies $\omega_i$

Observations:
- the normal frequencies correspond to the entire system oscilating together.
- symmetric motion has lower frequency than asymmetric motion
- The most symmetric motion will have the lowest frequency, typically:

$f=\sqrt{\frac{K}{M}}$

Where $K$ is effective spring constant and $M$ is total mass.

allNodeData.name: Damped Systems
allNodeData.description:
The equation of motion for a damped system is:

$0=m\ddot{x}+b\dot{x}+kx$

or 

$Acos(\omega t)=m\ddot{x}+b\dot{x}+kx$

in the driven case

Damping parameter - $\beta = \frac{b}{2m}$

Natural frequency - $\omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$

Resonant Frequency - $\omega_R = \sqrt{\omega_0^2-2\beta^2}$

Regimes:

Free Oscillation: $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$

$\beta^2 \lt \omega_0^2$ - Underdamped (system oscillates following an exponentially decreasing envelope)

Oscillations follow $x(t)=Ae^{-\beta t}cos(\omega_1 t - \delta)$
with $\omega_1^2 - \omega_0^2 - \beta^2$ (characteristic frequency).

$\beta^2 = \omega_0^2$ - Critically damped (intermediate case)

$\beta^2 \gt \omega_0^2$ - Underdamped (no oscillation, only expontential components [with real powers])

Without damping amplitude is:

$D\propto \frac{1}{\lvert \omega_0^2-\omega^2\rvert}$ which blows up when driving frequency approaches $\omega_0$

allNodeData.name: Pendulum
allNodeData.description:
$mL\ddot{\theta}=-mgsin\theta$

Small angles (most likely case) yields:

$m\ddot{x}=-\frac{mgx}{L}$

With $\omega=\sqrt{\frac{g}{L}}$

Extended bodies:

allNodeData.name: Bernoulli's Principle
allNodeData.description:
Only works with incompressible fluids

$P_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2+\rho g z_1=P_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2+\rho g z_2$

allNodeData.name: Buoyant Forces
allNodeData.description:
$F=\rho V g$

The force on an object in water is proportional to the Volume of the object and the density of the fluid being displaced.

Water density : $\frac{1g}{10cm^3}=\frac{1000 kg}{m^3}$

allNodeData.name: Maxwell's Equations
allNodeData.description:
$\nabla \cdot E=\frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0}$

$\nabla \cdot B = 0$

$\nabla \times E = \frac{\partial B}{\partial t}$

$\nabla \times B = \mu_0(\mathbf{J}+\epsilon_0\frac{\partial E}{\partial t})$

allNodeData.name: M.E. Integral Form
allNodeData.description:
$\oiint_\sigma \mathbf{E} \cdot d \mathbf{A}=\frac{Q}{\epsilon_0}$

$\oiint_\sigma \mathbf{B} \cdot d \mathbf{A}= 0$

$\oint_\lambda \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l}=-\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial t}$

$\oint_\lambda \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = \mu_0 I + \mu_0\epsilon_0\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial t}$

allNodeData.name: Electrostatics
allNodeData.description:
Electrostatics eliminates time dependence in which case (in the absence of magnetism), maxwell's laws reduce to:

$\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E} = \frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0}$

$\nabla \times E = 0 $ 

$\oint_\sigma E\cdot dS=\frac{Q}{\epsilon_0}$

$\oint_C E \cdot dl =0$

allNodeData.name: Electric Potential
allNodeData.description:
$\textbf{E} = -\nabla V$

Integrating through the potential yields:

$V(b) = - \int_a^b E \cdot dl$

Notes: 
-Potentials are always continuous
-The derivatives of potentials are continuous, except at charged surfaces.
-$V$ is constant through a conductor

allNodeData.name: Poisson's Equation
allNodeData.description: $-\nabla^2 V = \frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0}$

allNodeData.name: Solving for fields
allNodeData.description:
1. Figure out the symmetry of the problem
2. Find a gaussian surface
3. Solve for the field

Common examples:
 - spheres
 - shells
 - cylinders
 - line charges
 - dipole
 - sheets

allNodeData.name: Coulomb's Law
allNodeData.description:
For a point charge we have:

$E(r) = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0r^2}\hat{r}$

$V(r) = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0r}$

allNodeData.name: Boundary Conditions (E)
allNodeData.description:
The 2nd electrostatics formula tells us that, for a loop passing perpendicular but passing through a plane:

$E_{out}^\parallel-E_{in}^\parallel=0$

$E_{out}^\perp-E_{in}^\perp=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}$

Check for boundary conditions at surfaces of conductors/charged surfaces at the end of all problems to avoid making sign errors

allNodeData.name: Useful Integrals
allNodeData.description:
$\int_0^\pi sin(\theta)d\theta=2$
$\int_0^\pi sin^2(\theta)d\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}$
$\int_0^\pi sin^3(\theta)d\theta=\frac{4}{3}$

$\int_0^{2\pi} sin^2(\theta)d\theta=\pi$
$\int_0^{2\pi} sin^{n}(\theta)d\theta=0$ where $n$ is an odd integer.

Stokes:
$\oint_S (\nabla \times E) dS = \oint_C E \cdot dl$

Divergence Theorem:
$\oint_V (\nabla \cdot E) dV = \oint_S E \cdot dA$

Average value of $sin^2(\theta)$
$\braket{\sin^2\theta}=\frac{\int_0^{2\pi}sin^2\theta d\theta}{2\pi}=\frac{\pi}{2\pi}=\frac{1}{2}$

allNodeData.name: Conductors
allNodeData.description:
The charge in a conductor spreads out to the boundaries. As a result:
- $V$ is constant through a conductor.
- $E=0$ in the interior of a conductor.
- Net charge density $\rho_{net}=0$ inside a conductor.
- Any net charge is confined to the surface
- The electric field just outside a conductor is perpendicular to the surface.

Grounded Conductors:
- a grounded conductor is an infinite source and sink of charge
- it often serves are reference for potential, i.e. $V=0$.
- putting a charge near a grounded conductor surface will induce a charge on it. (see method of images)

allNodeData.name: Method of Images
allNodeData.description: Uniqueness implies that if you can guess $V$ and it is correct, it is the right potential. This can be exploited in the case where some charge configuration is positioned near an infinite grounded plane. In this case, potential must be constant, 0 actually, throughout the plane. Introducing a fake image charge of opposite sign and symmetrically placed across the plane exactly mimics this potential. That being said, work cannot be done on an image charge, as it is not real. Therefore to calculate E it is best to use the image configuration only to directly calculate E, rather than getting it from potential (which will implicitly count the work done on image charges).

allNodeData.name: Work and Energy in Electrostatics
allNodeData.description:
The work required to put together $n$ point charges is:

W=$\frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n q_i V(r_i)$

or in a continuous charge distribution:

$\frac{1}{2}\int\rho(r)V(r)d^3r$

There is energy stored in side fields as:

$U_E = \frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\int\lvert E \rvert^2 d^3r$

BEWARE: the energy associated with a point charge is infinite. This is because the $\frac{1}{r^2}$ term in the integral diverges at $r=0$. It is often better to find a $differential$ calculation for work done.

allNodeData.name: Capacitors
allNodeData.description:
Two parallel plates with charges $Q$ and $-Q$ on them. 

$Q = CV$

between 2 parallel plates (infinite)
$C= \frac{A\epsilon_0}{d}$

Energy stored in a capacitor:

$U_E = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$

allNodeData.name: Magnetostatics
allNodeData.description:
Generally use the following equations in the absence of dynamic electric fields.

$\nabla \cdot B = 0$

$\nabla \times B = \mu_0 J$ (magnetostatics)

Integral form:

$\oint_S B \cdot dS = 0$

$\oint_C B \cdot dl = \mu_0 I_{enc}$ (magnetostatics)


3 classes of problems:
- Finding the field due to a configuration of currents
- Finding forces on wires or charges due to fields
- Finding energies of fields

allNodeData.name: Magnetic Potential
allNodeData.description:
Since $\nabla \times B \ne 0$ we cannot use a scalar potential, so we define the vector potential of magnetic fields as:

$\nabla \times A = B$

It is very unlikely that a vector potential question is asked on the GRE.

allNodeData.name: Lorentz Force Law
allNodeData.description:
On test charges in a magnetic field:

$F_B = qv \times B$

and differential form:

$dF_B = Idl\times B$

Note that $I = \frac{dq}{dt}$

allNodeData.name: Ampere's Law
allNodeData.description:
When the problem has a high degree of symmetry, specifically when a curve can be generated around some enclosed current (see magnetic field around a current carrying wire), and B is constant through the whole loop, we can use:

$\oint_C B \cdot dl = \mu_0 I_{enc}$

$\lvert B \rvert \oint_C dl = \mu_0 I_{enc}$

allNodeData.name: Biot-Savart Law
allNodeData.description: $B(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\int \frac{dl \times \hat{r}'}{r'^2}$

allNodeData.name: Common current configurations
allNodeData.description:
Wires
Ampere law for infinite
Biot-Savart for finite (use angles and $x=\frac{d}{cos\theta}$)
Solenoids
Use ampere law and draw box perpendicular to windings. all but the center cancel out and you get $BL=\mu_0 I N$
Toroids
Wrapping the solenoid fully around now gives (through the application of the ampere law through the plane of the toroid):

$B = \frac{\mu_0 NI}{2\pi r}$

Note this now has an $r$ dependence and this result is independent of geometry.

allNodeData.name: Boundary Conditions (B)
allNodeData.description:
At the surface of a boundary through which some current density $K$ is present:

$B_{out}^\perp-B_{in}^\perp = 0$

$B_{out}^\parallel-B_{in}^\parallel=\mu_0 K \times \hat{n}$

allNodeData.name: Work and Energy in Magnetostatics
allNodeData.description:
Magnetic fields do NO WORK, this is because the forces they cause never act in the direction of motion of a charge.

Energy is stored in magnetic fields via:

$U_B = \frac{1}{2\mu_0}\int\lvert B \rvert^2 d^3r$

allNodeData.name: Cyclotron Motion
allNodeData.description:
When a charged particle is moving through a magnetic field we can induce a uniform circular motion due to the magnetic field and the lorentz force:

$qvB = \frac{mv^2}{r}$

$qB = \frac{mv}{r}$

Substituting $\omega = \frac{v}{r}$ we get the cyclotron frequency:

$\omega = \frac{qB}{m}$

allNodeData.name: Electrodynamics
allNodeData.description: Requires time dependent forms of Maxwell's equations

allNodeData.name: Faraday's Law
allNodeData.description:
$\oint_C E \cdot dl = -\frac{d \Phi_B}{d t}$

This is often called the emf (it is an electric $potential$ not a field):

$\mathcal{E}=-\frac{d \Phi_B}{d t}$

Where $\Phi_B = \int_S B \cdot dS$ is the magnetic $flux$ through a surface.

The minus sign in these equations is often called "Lenz's Law" and ensures that the induced magnetic field by the (induced) current in the wire opposes the external magnetic field.

allNodeData.name: Inductors
allNodeData.description:
The self-inductance is defined to be the constant L in the expression:

$\phi_B = L I$

For the loop of wire this means that that magnetic flux perpendicular to the loop is proportional to the current via the constant $L$. This can also be shown with the differential form.

$\mathcal{E} = -L\frac{dI}{dt}$

The energy stored in an inductor is:

$U_L=\frac{1}{2}LI^2$

allNodeData.name: Common L values
allNodeData.description:
$L_{solenoid} = \frac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{l}$

The $N^2$ term is due to multiple windings contributing to the flux term.

allNodeData.name: Electric Dipoles
allNodeData.description:
The dipole moment is defined as:

$\vec{p} = q_1\vec{r_1}-q_2\vec{r_2}=q\vec{d}$

Where $\vec{d}$ is the vector from the $negative$ to the $positive$ charges.

The dipole moment for groups of charges is:

$\vec{p} = \sum\limits_i q_i\vec{r_i}$

or for continuous distributions:

$\vec{p} = \int_V \rho(\vec{r})\vec{r} dV$

allNodeData.name: Dipole Potentials (E)
allNodeData.description:
The potential of a dipole is:

$V(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{\vec{p}\cdot\hat{r}}{r^2}$

Note that it goes as $\frac{1}{r^2}$

allNodeData.name: Dipole Torque
allNodeData.description:
Since dipoles have 0 net electric charge, they do not experience translational forces, they do however experience torque which goes as:

$\vec{N} = \vec{p}\times \vec{E}$

which gives rise to a potential associated with the misalignment of a dipole with a surrounding electric field of:

$U = -\vec{p} \cdot \vec{E}$

allNodeData.name: Magnetic Dipoles
allNodeData.description:
These cannot be composed of monopoles, and are instead constructed with loops of wire yielding magnetic dipole moments of:

$\vec{m}=I\vec{A}$

This yields a corresponding Torque of:

$\vec{N} = \vec{m} \times \vec{B}$

and potential of:

$U = -\vec{m} \cdot \vec{B}$

allNodeData.name: Multipole Expansion
allNodeData.description:
Unlikely to be asked:

$V(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\sum\limits_{n=0}^\infty \frac{1}{r^{n+1}}\int(r')P_n(cos\theta')\rho(r')d^3r'$

allNodeData.name: Terminology
allNodeData.description:
"Small angle": use the approximations:

$\sin\theta=\theta$ and $\tan\theta = \theta$

allNodeData.name: Matter Effects
allNodeData.description: Unlikely to be asked, last 3 exams had 1 question each regarding capcitors/dielectrics.

allNodeData.name: Polarization
allNodeData.description:
Bound charges are a way to parameterize polarization in which the induced dipoles:

Surface charge:

$\sigma_b = \vec{P} \cdot \hat{n}$

Volume charge:

$\rho_b = -\nabla \cdot \vec{P}$

where $\vec{P}$ is the polarization.

Note that in the case of a volume charge, we are looking for the $divergence$ of $\vec{P}$, so in the case of a uniform polarization field, there is no induced bound volume charge.

allNodeData.name: Dielectrics
allNodeData.description:
Dielectrics are materials that can be slightly polarized by external electric fields to cancel out some of the field.

Most likely to be asked about a capacitor with a dielectric which has form:

$\epsilon_0 \to \epsilon = k\epsilon_0$

$C = \frac{\epsilon A}{d} = k\frac{\epsilon_0 A}{d}$

Where $k$ is the dielectric constant of the material.

allNodeData.name: Electromagnetic Waves
allNodeData.description:
Manipulating Maxwell's Equations for a vacuum we get:

$\nabla^2 B = \mu_0\epsilon_0\frac{\partial ^2 B}{\partial t^2}$

$\nabla^2 E = \mu_0\epsilon_0\frac{\partial ^2 E}{\partial t^2}$

and we find that $c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}}$

The solutions of these equations take the form:

$\tilde{E}(r)=\tilde{E}_0e^{i(\vec{k}\cdot\vec{r}-\omega t)}\hat{n}$

$\tilde{B}(r)=\frac{1}{c}\tilde{E}_0e^{i(\vec{k}\cdot\vec{r}-\omega t)}(\hat{k}\times\hat{n})$

Here $\hat{n}$ is the polarization direction (direction of the Electric component of the wave, $\hat{k}$ is the direction of propagation for the EM wave, the direction of the magnetic component of the wave is governed by the right hand rule. This makes EM waves $transverse$ waves. Note that $\tilde{E}_0$ can be complex, but the physical parts of the wave are the real components of those equations, i.e. $Re(\tilde{E})$

When an EM wave is normally incident on a conductor, the reflected wave has the same direction of magnetic component and the opposite electric component direction.

allNodeData.name: Poynting Vector
allNodeData.description:
The poynting vector gives the flux of energy of the wave:

$S=\frac{1}{\mu_0}(E\times B)$

or for real fields:

$S = \frac{1}{2\mu_0}Re(\tilde{E}\times\tilde{B}^*)$

Using the fact that the average of $sin^2\theta$ and $cos^2\theta$ over 1 period is $\frac{1}{2}$, we get that:

$I=\braket{S}=\frac{1}{2}c\epsilon_0 E^2_0$

Note that intensity is average power per unit area.

allNodeData.name: Accelerating Charges
allNodeData.description:
Accelerating charges radiate an energy of:

$P=\frac{q^2a^2}{6\pi\epsilon_0 c^3}=\frac{\mu_0 q^2 a^2}{6\pi c}$

where $q$ is charge and $a$ is acceleration.

allNodeData.name: Dipole Radiation
allNodeData.description:
An oscillating electric dipole with momentum:

$p(t)=p_0cos(\omega t)\hat{z}$

will radiate with intensity:

$\braket{S} = (\frac{\mu_0 p_0^2 \omega^4}{32\pi^2 c}\frac{sin^2\theta}{r^2})$

and power:

$\braket{P}_E = \frac{\mu_0 p_0^2 \omega^4}{12\pi c}$

Similarly

Oscillating magnetic dipoles radiate with power:

$\braket{P}_B = \frac{\mu_0 m_0^2 \omega^4}{12\pi c^3}$

Key takeaways:

 - monopoles do not radiate
 - electric dipole radiation dominates of magnetic dipole radiation
 - mostly understand the proportionalities and relations not necessarily the exact prefactors.

allNodeData.name: Circuits
allNodeData.description:
$V_R = IR$

$V_C = \frac{Q}{C}$

$V_L = L \frac{dI}{dt}$

Inductors are added like capacitors.

Resistivity $\rho$:

$R = \frac{\rho l}{A}$

where $l$ is length and $A$ is cross sectional area.

Dissipation of energy through resistor:

$P=IV=I^2R=\frac{V^2}{R}$

Energy Storage:

$U_C = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$

$U_L = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$

allNodeData.name: Kirchhoff's Rules
allNodeData.description:
Sum of currents at any given node is 0

Sum of voltages around any closed loop is 0

allNodeData.name: Common Circuits
allNodeData.description:
RC with no voltage source:

$0=R\frac{dQ}{dt} + \frac{1}{C}Q$

RL circuit with voltage source:

$V = IR + L\frac{dI}{dt}$

if voltage is switched off current becomes:

$I=\frac{V}{R}(1-e^-\frac{R}{L}t)$

RLC single components not driven: 
This is a damped oscillatory solution of the form:

$0=L\ddot{x}+R\dot{x}+\frac{1}{C}x$

LC circuit:
$\omega_0 \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$

allNodeData.name: The Wave Equation
allNodeData.description:
The general wave equation is:

$\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial t^2}=v^2\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}$

Solutions are of the form:

$f(x\pm vt)$ which represents some fixed disturbance propagating either to the left or right with constant speed $v$.

The linearity of this equation is such that if any two functions $f$ and $g$ are solutions, so too is $f+g$

Traveling wave solutions are of form $f(x-vt)$ while standing wave solutions are of form $f(x,t)=A(x)B(t)$

allNodeData.name: General Wave
allNodeData.description:
The most general functional form of a wave is:

$f(x,t) = Acos(kx-\omega t+\delta)$

Where:
$k$ - wavenumber
$A$ - Amplitude
$\omega$ - angular frequency
$\delta$ - phase offset

The energy of a wave is proportional to $A^2$

The wavenumber $k$ is sort of the $spatial$ frequency where:

$\lambda = \frac{2\pi}{k}$

The angular frequency $\omega$ is the $temporal$ frequency with:

$T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}$, $2\pi f=\omega$

The complex form gives:

$f(x,t) = Re(Ae^{i(kx-\omega t)})$

or for a wave traveling in 3 dimensions:

$f(x,t) = Re(Ae^{i(\vec{k}\cdot\vec{r}-\omega t)})$

where $\vec{k}$ is the $wavevector$ defining both the direction and of which $\lvert \vec{k} \rvert=k$

allNodeData.name: Dispersion
allNodeData.description:
For the simplest waves satisfying the basic wave equation:

$\omega = vk$
$v = hf$

More complicated waves which include changes in medium, frictional dissipation and other things will still adhere to a dispersion relation.

The case where $\omega(k)=vk$ is called $linear$ dispersion (light in a vacuum obeys this).

Phase velocity: $\frac{\omega}{k}$ (velocity of individual wave crest)

Group velocity: $\frac{d\omega}{dk}$ (velocity of wave packet)

In the case of linear dispersion these quantities are the same.

Note that information travels at the group velocity.

allNodeData.name: Examples of Wave dispersion
allNodeData.description:
For a vibrating string we have:

$v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$

and for sound we have

$c_s = \sqrt{\frac{K}{\rho}}$

allNodeData.name: Index of refraction
allNodeData.description:
Index of refraction $n$ is the factor by which the speed of light is reduced in a medium:

$\frac{\omega}{k} = \frac{c}{n}$

In fact, the wavelength remains the same and it is actually:

$\lambda \to \frac{\lambda}{n}$

Real materials do not have constant $n$ but this will not show up on the GRE

allNodeData.name: Polarization (light)
allNodeData.description:
A wave is $polarized$ if the source emits waves with the same $\hat{n}$

When the propagation direction is perpendicular to the polarization, we have a transverse wave, if it is parallel, we have a longitudinal wave.

Two common applications on the GRE:

Malus' Law:

Consider light of intensity $I_0$ and polarization $\hat{n}$ incident on a filter which only emits light polarized along $\hat{n_0}$, then the light exits with intensity:

$I = I_0cos^2\theta$,    where $\theta=\hat{n}\cdot\hat{n}_0$

Unpolarized light incident upon a polarized filter yields the average value of $I$ over all angles: $\braket{I}=I_0\frac{\int_0^{2\pi}cos^2\theta}{2\pi}=\frac{I_0}{2}$

allNodeData.name: Brewster's Angle
allNodeData.description:
Unpolarized light incident upon a material interface where one material has $n_1$ and the other $n_2$ will, at some angle $\theta_B$ (relative to the normal) be entirely reflected $and$ completely polarized perpendicular to the plane formed by the incident ray and the normal to the surface.

$\theta_B = \arctan({\frac{n_2}{n_1}})$

allNodeData.name: Inteference
allNodeData.description:
Constructive interference occurs at phase differences of $2\pi n$
Destructive interference occurs at phase differences of $\pi + 2\pi n$

allNodeData.name: Double Slit Diffraction
allNodeData.description:
Consider two slits $d$ apart with monochromatic light shining through to a screen a distance $L$ away. If $L\gt\gt d$ then we can approximate the paths as parallel, and then the only path difference becomes $d sin\theta$. Then this path difference $\Delta x$ is a multiple of the wavelength, we will get constructive interference, when it is a half multiple, we will get destructive:

Constructive: $d sin\theta = \lambda n$

Destructive: $d sin\theta = \frac{\lambda}{2}+\lambda n = (\frac{1}{2}+n)\lambda$

Note that the center is a Maxima since the waves follow the same distance

allNodeData.name: Single Slit Diffraction
allNodeData.description:
Consider monochromatic light passing through a slit of width $a$ to a screen a distance $L$ away:

Minima occur at: $a sin\theta = n\lambda$

The exception is the single maximum at the center $n=0$

Note that we must have $\lambda$ on the same order as $a$

allNodeData.name: Optical Pathlength
allNodeData.description:
As light travels through a medium of index of refraction $n$, it slows down accordingly as $\frac{c}{n}$. We then define the optical pathlength $\Delta x$ as"

$\Delta x = nd$

That is, we parameterize this slowing by stretching the path the light took.

Tis is because for some wave traveling through length $d$ in vacuum, the argument of the oscillatory function increased by:

$\delta_v = \frac{2 \pi d}{\lambda}$

But in the medium with index of refraction $n$ we have $\lambda \to \frac{\lambda}{n}$ thus:

$\delta_n = \frac{2 \pi d}{\frac{\lambda}{n}}=\frac{2n\pi d}{\lambda}$

allNodeData.name: Thin films
allNodeData.description:
If a light traveling through a medium of $n_1$ strikes an interface with a medium of $n_2$ and reflects, we see a phase shift of:

$\delta: \begin{cases}\pi, && n_2\gt n_1\\0, && n_2 \lt n_1\end{cases}$

Generally these problems involve calculating the phase shift of light incident on a thin film, just remember to account for indices of refraction and geometrical phase shifts + the possible phase shift from reflection.

allNodeData.name: Misc. Diffraction
allNodeData.description:
Circular diffraction:

First circular diffraction minima: $Dsin\theta = 1.22\lambda$

This is the Rayleigh criterion and it tells us the minimum angle for us to be able to resolve 2 objects as distinct. Note here that $\theta$ is the total angle subtended by the circular projection, not just from the middle line to the top.

Bragg Diffraction:

Maxima: $dsin\theta = \frac{n\lambda}{2}$

Note here that $\theta$ is the angle of ray incidence to the horizontal

allNodeData.name: Geometric Optics
allNodeData.description:
If the wavelength of the light is large compared to the objects it is interacting with, the effects of phase shifts can be ignored. When a wave hits an interface between materials of differing indices of refraction, we have:

Reflection: $\theta_i = \theta_r$

Refraction: $n_1 sin\theta_1 = n_2 sin \theta_2$

where $\theta$ values are defined relative the the interfaces normal.

allNodeData.name: Lenses and Mirrors
allNodeData.description:
The most important equation for geometric optics is:

$\frac{1}{s}+\frac{1}{s'} = \frac{1}{f}$

$f$ represents focal length (the distance from the surface of an optical instrument to its focus)

Note: In geometric optics:
all incident light rays parallel to the axis are reflected or refracted through the focus, and all light rays passing through the focus are either reflected or refracted so that they come out parallel to the axis.

For a spherical mirror: $f=\frac{R}{2}$

$s$ is the position of an object and $s'$ is the position of the image created by the optical equipment.

Positive distances $\implies$ same side as light rays (incoming for $s$,outgoing for $s'$

Negative distances $\implies$ opposite side as light rays (incoming for $s$,outgoing for $s'$

$s'$ is positive is the image is $real$ (it is created by actual light rays) and negative if it is $virtual$ (formed on the opposite side of the optical instrument from the outgoing light rays).

allNodeData.name: Lensmaker's equation
allNodeData.description:
$\frac{1}{f} = (n-1)(\frac{1}{R_1}-\frac{1}{R_2})$

The sign convention here is such that $f$ is positive for converging lenses and negative for diverging lenses.

allNodeData.name: Magnification
allNodeData.description:
$m=-\frac{s'}{s}$

$\lvert m \rvert$ is the ratio of the sizes of the images while the sign indicated if the image is upright (m is positive) or upside down (m is negative).

allNodeData.name: Rayleigh Scattering
allNodeData.description:
Applicable when the wavelength scale of incident light is much smaller than the scale of the object being hit (like a molecule)

$I \propto I_0\lambda^{-4}q^6$

allNodeData.name: Assorted Topics In Optics and Waves
Doppler Effect
allNodeData.description:
$f = \frac{v+v_r}{v-v_s}f_0$

Here subscripts stand for reciever and source respectfully and v is the velocity of the wave.

Note: $v_r$ and $v_s$ are both: positive if approaching, and negative if moving away from eachother.

Note that this only applies at nonrelativistic speeds and if the source and receiver are moving directly towards eachother, else we must take just the component of velocity approaching/receding$

allNodeData.name: Standing Sound Waves
allNodeData.description:
Open ends are nodes (0 average pressure difference with atmosphere)

Closed ends are antinodes (maximum average pressure difference with atmosphere)

most helpful is to draw a diagram, find the lowest possible frequency by drawing a trig function with its lowest amplitude at open ends and highest at closed ends, then simply increase the frequencies such that those boundary conditions remain sastisfied.

allNodeData.name: Trig Phases
allNodeData.description: $sin(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta) = cos(\theta)$
